newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: E.Asia Oilseeds- S.Korea buyers wait for NLCF move.
newsitem.headline: E.Asia Oilseeds- S.Korea buyers wait for NLCF move.

text.p: South Korean oilseeds and feeds buyers are waiting for the results of the National Livestock Cooperatives Federation's (NLCF) re-tenders on Tuesday in soymeal, feed wheat and other feeds, before re-entering the market traders said on Monday.

The NLCF is to re-invite tenders to buy 40,000 tonnes of soymeal, 52,000 tonnes of feed wheat, 30,000 tonnes of tapioca hard pellets and 14,000 tonnes of rapeseed meal on Tuesday after passing last Friday due to higher offer prices.
"If the NLCF buys soymeal and feed wheat through tenders on Tuesday, other buyers may follow to cover their needs," a trader with a Seoul-based foreign trading firm said.
However, buying interest in feed wheat would be limited by current lower corn prices, the trader added.

He said several South Korean buyers were seen seeking about two 30,000-tonne cargoes of soymeal for arrival in September and October. But other local feed mills are looking to alternative meals and feeds to partially substitute for their soymeal requirement as international soymeal prices extend recent gains.

Traders said three major South Korean soybean crushers are likely to return to the U.S. market to cover their needs for August shipment, despite the recent rally in prices, as the Brazilian export season is coming to an end.
The soybean crushers include Cheiljedang Corp and Shindongbang Corp with requirements of 35,000-50,000 tonnes per month each and Sam Yang Foods Co Ltd with 15,000 tonnes.
In Japan, U.S. soybean buyers are expected to maintain a low profile this week as old crop prices are still significantly above new crop, traders said.
They added said that uncertainty over Japan's soymeal demand for the third quarter is also causing buyers to hold back.
Japanese importers have already finished covering U.S. soybean for July shipment.
"We're going to trim U.S. our soybean buying until September shipment. It's better to wait for new crop, rather than buying expensive old crop," an official at an edible oil maker said.
